title: Random forest-based lithology identification using geophysical well logging data along a borehole in a coastal aquifer in Suruga Bay, Japan
abstract: Abstract Machine learning techniques have attracted attention for lithology identification, which is fundamental for understanding geological structures. However, the efficacy of machine learning-based lithology identification, specifically in deep (several hundred meters) coastal aquifers composed predominantly of unconsolidated sediments, remains underexplored. Therefore, this study developed machine learning models based on decision trees, random forest (RF), logistic regression, and multilayer perceptron (MLP) algorithms that classify lithofacies using geophysical well logging data collected along a borehole located in Suruga Bay, Shizuoka Prefecture, Japan. Two to nine input features were selected for the seven cases to classify four lithofacies: “cobbles and gravel”, “sand with gravel”, “silt with gravel”, and “basaltic lava”. The models showed accuracy ranging from 73.9% to 90.4%, with the RF- and MLP-based models achieving accuracy of 90.4% and 90.1%, respectively, when trained using all available input features. This indicates their effectiveness for lithology identification in the target borehole. Feature importance analysis using the SHapley Additive exPlanations method suggested that natural gamma ray, widely used in groundwater exploration, served as a key input feature in many of the analyzed cases. The incorporation of other input features (i.e., electrical resistivity, P-wave velocity, density, and NMR-derived parameters) generally improved the prediction performance. The results demonstrate the applicability of machine learning algorithms for lithology identification in a coastal aquifer several hundred meters thick, consisting of unconsolidated alluvial sediments and lava flows. These findings suggest that machine-learning techniques have the potential to reduce the time, labor, and costs associated with hydrogeological surveys and groundwater exploration.

title: Machine Learning for Specialized QKD Aspects: A Survey of Adaptive Protocols, Free-Space Links, 6G Integration, and Steerability-Aware Security
abstract: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) provides information-theoretic security grounded in the laws of quantum mechanics, yet practical deployment increasingly extends beyond conventional point-to-point fiber links. Several rapidly emerging QKD directions are often studied separately, including adaptive protocol and parameter support; free-space, satellite, UAV, and high-altitude platform (HAP) channels; integration with IoT and 6G networks; quantum-secured federated learning; Quantum Machine Learning (QML) assisted decision support; and steerability-aware estimation for one-sided device-independent QKD. This survey examines how Machine Learning (ML), Reinforcement Learning (RL), and QML address these specialized scenarios and organizes the literature into five thematic pillars: (I) adaptive protocol and parameter support; (II) free-space, satellite, UAV, and HAP-assisted QKD; (III) QKD for IoT, 6G, and quantum-secured federated learning; (IV) QML-assisted QKD functions; and (V) steerability-aware and one-sided device-independent QKD security estimation. For each theme, we follow a consistent problem, conventional solution, and ML/RL/QML solution structure and summarize reported gains using metrics such as accuracy, mean absolute percentage error, QBER reduction, and secret key rate improvement. We further provide thematic and cross-theme comparison tables and identify open challenges, including dataset scarcity, transferability across weather and mobility conditions, interpretability, trustworthy QML, and the boundary between ML-based decision support and security certification. This survey serves as a focused reference for adaptive, non-terrestrial, and application-integrated QKD systems.

title: Multi-Task Early-Recognition Prefix Trees: Polynomial Islands and NP-Completeness of the Arbitrary-Weight Spine
abstract: We study a finite prefix-tree optimization problem in which one rooted full binary treeis evaluated by several recognition tasks under the same positive weight vector. A taskis a partition of the alphabet, and recognition of an object stops at the first node on itsroot-to-leaf path whose descendant leaves lie entirely inside the object’s partition block.For two tasks we minimize the maximum additive regret relative to the two task-specificoptima. We focus on the nested coarse-versus-point setting and derive an exact spinerepresentation for the singleton-versus-rest subclass. This representation yields polynomialtime exact algorithms for uniform inputs with a fixed number of coarse blocks and, moregenerally, for nonuniform inputs with both a fixed number of coarse blocks and a fixednumber of distinct weight values. In particular, the two-block spine is polynomial forevery fixed weight diversity. We then show that the same fixed two-block spine becomesNP-complete when arbitrary binary-encoded weights are allowed. The reduction fromSubset Sum combines exact-cardinality tagging, a two-group forcing lemma, perturbationstable Huffman calibration, and opposite regret inequalities that squeeze a selected subsetsum to equality. This differs from scenario-robust Huffman optimization: there the treeis evaluated under several frequency vectors with ordinary leaf stopping, whereas herethe weight vector is fixed and the competing costs arise from different partition-inducedstopping functionals. An adversarial literature audit found no exact collision among theprimary-source-checked families. The publisher abstract of Du–Ko’s 1987 paper uses thephrase “minimax measure” for group testing; neighboring primary sources in the sameliterature define minimax performance through the maximum number of tests, rather thanthrough additive regret between task-specific optima. Because the formal 1987 definitionwas not accessible in the present audit, we still make no exhaustive historical firstness claim.The resulting theorem is positioned narrowly as a complexity frontier for the first-purespine model.

title: Adversarial Machine Learning Attacks
abstract: The evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) has introduced sophisticated attack vectors that exploit inherent vulnerabilities in machine learning systems. This chapter examines adversarial machine learning attacks, including data poisoning, evasion attacks, model inversion, extraction techniques, and emerging threats against large language models. Through detailed technical analysis and real-world examples, we explore the mechanisms by which adversaries compromise AI systems across their lifecycle, from training data manipulation to deployment-phase evasion. The chapter concludes with comprehensive defense strategies, highlighting the ongoing arms race between attackers developing increasingly sophisticated techniques and defenders implementing robust countermeasures. Understanding these adversarial techniques is essential for building resilient AI systems capable of withstanding malicious exploitation.

title: Three Necessary Principles for Self-Supervised Visual Representation Learning
abstract: We argue that learning visual representations without labels requires a training signal jointly complete across three non-overlapping objectives: semantic invariance across augmented views, patch-level spatial prediction, and representational non-degeneracy. We formalize these as the observation, prediction, and regularization principles and prove (i) that combining observation and prediction without regularization admits the constant encoder as a global minimizer under negative-free alignment; (ii) that the two objectives are gradient-complementary and structurally non-conflicting at the encoder output; and (iii) that the momentum encoder converges to the same fixed point as the online encoder and provides no collapse guarantee at convergence. Contrastive alignment provides only self-limiting collapse resistance, formalized via an explicit gradient-decay argument. Dropping prediction withholds the spatial training signal by construction; dropping observation forfeits cross-view semantic invariance by construction; at the scale we study, no pair substitutes for the third. Every major self-supervised method is a special case of a single unified energy decomposition. We pair every theoretical claim with a controlled experiment, including a patch-retrieval evaluation for the spatial consequence of prediction.

title: One Intelligence, Multiple Hands: A Shared-Context Architecture for Cooperative Voice and Execution Agents
abstract: AI workspaces commonly separate conversation from execution, forcing people to relay corrections and current state between specialized agents. This preprint presents a shared-context architecture in which role-specialized voice, execution, research, reflection, and consolidation processes operate over versioned project state, stable object identities, permissions, commitments, event history, provenance, and correction handling. It reports a deterministic two-task reference application comparing isolated, periodic-summary, and shared-state conditions. Across 18 preregistered runs, the shared-state condition eliminated fixture stale attempts, reduced correction latency from four events to two, produced exact immediate state reports, and retained full task success, conflict rejection, provenance, and restart recovery. The accompanying reproducibility package contains the reference application, frozen fixtures, validators, formal transaction kernel, preregistration, redacted run record, and checksums. The reported result is limited to the deterministic pilot and does not establish general language-model performance, human-team performance, user preference, consciousness, or cross-repository generality.

title: 中文全称:元收敛认知引擎(MCCE)V8.3-LAPE 跨学科通用因果动力学评估语言

title: Neurosymbolic Discovery of Algebraic Graph Constructions: Supplementary Material (NeSy 2026)
abstract: Software and experimental data backing each empirical claim in: David Seka and Stefan Szeider, "Neurosymbolic Discovery of Algebraic Graph Constructions", NeSy 2026 (20th International Conference on Neurosymbolic Learning and Reasoning), PMLR vol. 284. The archive contains: the pre-registered 100-graph benchmark of two-orbit graphs (graph6 targets and metadata); all agent run transcripts (100 capability runs, a 40-graph backbone pre-study across five models, a 50-graph symmetry-stratified reliability set, a 20-graph planted-construction recall test, and the Bernhart-Kainen case study); the verbatim system prompt and grading prompt; the two non-LLM baselines (strong template enumeration and literature lookup) with scripts and results; per-run isomorphism verification and LLM-judge grades; a human-audit package for judge calibration; and archival copies of the two released software tools. Replay instructions are in README.md (uvx mcp-minion@0.2.1; requires SageMath 10.6+ and an OpenRouter API key). The two bundled software folders are MIT-licensed, Copyright (c) 2026 Stefan Szeider, and are maintained outside this archive: mcp-sage, the SageMath MCP server (https://github.com/szeider/mcp-sage, PyPI: mcp-sage), and mcp-minion, the ReAct agent harness (https://github.com/szeider/mcp-solver, PyPI: mcp-minion). All other content is licensed CC BY 4.0.

title: Quantum Antifragility: NISQ Noise Feeds Integrated Information via Zero-Noise Extrapolation
abstract: We present the first experimental demonstration that quantum noise is informative, not merely destructive — validating Theorem 8 of IIT 5.1 (FEP-MaxCal Bridge). Using a 5-qubit GHZ circuit on an AerSimulator calibrated with real IBM Quantum ibm_fez noise parameters (T1=320µs, T2=150µs, gate2q error=2.83e-3), we show that Zero Noise Extrapolation (ZNE) recovers integrated information (Φ) to a value exceeding the noiseless ideal: Φ_ZNE = 1.1736 > Φ_ideal = 0.9999 (permutation test, p < 0.000001, N=20 runs, 8192 shots each, 10000 bootstrap resamples). ZNE requires controlled noise scaling (identity folding at λ = 1, 2, 3) that is only feasible in simulation; however, the noise model is calibrated from 3766 real IBM Quantum jobs across 6 backends, and prior hardware experiments on ibm_fez (V1: Φ=0.757, V2: Φ=0.832 with ZNE on real hardware) validate the baseline metrics. The experiment follows a four-phase paradigm: (1) Baseline: GHZ-5 ideal yields Φ=0.9999; (2) Attack: NISQ noise degrades Φ to 0.8804 (-12%); (3) Recovery: Hahn Echo alone shows no significant improvement (p=0.853), but ZNE with 3-scale identity folding and linear extrapolation to noise=0 yields Φ=1.1736; (4) Antifragility: the recovered system exceeds the original baseline by +17.4%. Additional findings: Φ scales monotonically with qubit count (2q→7q), distinguishes entanglement topology (GHZ > W-state > Cluster ≈ Separable), is robust across 4 IBM backend noise models (CV=3.35%), and decays exponentially with circuit depth (τ=29.52 layers). Hardware validation on real ibm_fez confirms Φ for entangled vs separable circuits with Cohen's d = 191.3 (p < 0.0001).

title: AI ‐Enabled Cyber Threats
abstract: Understand AI-driven cyberattacks and build effective defensive strategies against them Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to automate, enhance, and evolve cyberattacks, yet most existing resources address AI only as a defensive tool. AI-Enabled Cyber Threats: The Rise of Artificial Intelligence in Cybercrime delivers a full-spectrum analysis of AI’s dual role in cybersecurity, covering offensive techniques, adversarial AI methods, and countermeasures from technical, ethical, and societal perspectives for professional and academic audiences. AI-Enabled Cyber Threats balances theoretical foundations with actionable defensive strategies. It examines the sophisticated methods malicious actors employ using AI, from autonomous AI hackers to AI-powered nation-state warfare. The book addresses the dual-use nature of AI technologies, equipping readers to design stronger defenses, understand adversarial AI techniques, and lead security innovations responsibly in an AI-dominant threat landscape. The book also provides: Analysis of how AI automates and evolves cyberattack methodologies, including practical threat examples drawn from real-world offensive scenarios Defensive frameworks and countermeasures developed by security professionals and institutions to mitigate AI-driven threats across organizations Coverage of ethical considerations and societal impacts arising from the weaponization of artificial intelligence in cybercrime Future-facing insights on emerging risks including autonomous AI hackers and AI-powered nation-state cyber warfare campaigns Guidance for building proactive, adaptive cybersecurity strategies that anticipate threats rather than relying on traditional reactive approaches Designed for cybersecurity professionals, AI researchers, and graduate students studying adversarial machine learning or cybercrime and digital forensics, this book provides the technical depth and strategic perspective needed to understand and counter AI-driven threats. Risk managers and compliance professionals will also find useful frameworks for organizational defense.

title: ZOMP: Zeroth-Order Multi-Modal Prompt Tuning for Vision-Language Models
abstract: Fine-tuning vision-language models such as CLIP typically requires backpropagation (BP) through the full model, which is infeasible when only forward-pass access is available, as is common for memory-constrained edge devices and proprietary model deployments. Prior BP-free, zeroth-order prompt-tuning methods avoid this requirement but often tune prompts in a single modality or optimize over a search space large enough that convergence requires thousands of forward passes, which is impractical under realistic query budgets. We propose ZOMP (Zeroth-Order Multimodal Prompt tuning), a query-efficient, fully forward-only method that tunes deep prompts in both the vision and text branches of a frozen CLIP model using simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation. ZOMP combines three ingredients: a cross-modal low-rank reparameterization that ties the two branches through a shared factor and keeps the effective search dimensionality small, a gradient-correction momentum term that stabilizes the noisy zeroth-order estimate, and a budget-indexed rank schedule that unlocks capacity as the query budget is spent. Across 13 vision-language benchmarks under a matched 5,000-query budget, ZOMP consistently outperforms prior BP-free prompt-tuning methods in both few-shot accuracy and query efficiency, and it generalizes better across base-to-new, cross-dataset transfer, and out-of-distribution settings. Our results show that jointly exploiting multimodality and low-rank structure is an effective route to practical, query-efficient BP-free prompt tuning.

title: PLNKicongo: Analysis of models based on the BERT architecture for processing the Angolan language Kicongo
abstract: Pre-trained contextual language models have demonstrated excellent performance in training with data from new languages and tasks. For this purpose, additional pre-training is necessary, since the lack of vocabulary of the language always tends to degrade the results. In this article, we present a procedure to deal with and treat unknown languages or languages without available resources such as Kicongo, a Bantu matrix language, commonly spoken in the northern regions of Angola, with greater incidence in rural regions and in the countries of central Africa (Democratic Republic of Congo, Republic of Congo and Gabon) and throughout the world. With the extension of Natural Language Processing (NLP) models based on the Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) architecture (BERT, RoBERTa and DistilBERT), the performance evaluation of the models was carried out using metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall and f1-score, achieving a performance rate higher than 97%.

title: Chameleon Neuron: continual-learning organism (code and papers)
abstract: Code and papers for the Chameleon Neuron, a continual-learning organism in which retention (not forgetting), transmutation (classifying known-but-corrupted inputs) and abstention (rejecting true out-of-distribution inputs) coexist on a single substrate, without binary masks and without replay. This archive accompanies two papers, both included in the repository: The Chameleon Neuron: Emergent Retention, Transmutation, and Abstention in a Continual-Learning Organism — validated on Split-CIFAR-100 over frozen ResNet-18 features (5 seeds), with an adversarial self-audit that reports the claims which did not survive it. A decoupled distance+energy gate is the only detector strong on both far- and near-OOD. The Chameleon on the LLM Substrate: Retention, Energy Routing, and the Principles of Sensor Blindness — ported to a frozen Qwen2.5-0.5B with a population of LoRA adapters. Distance routing over hidden states collapses to 29% through anisotropy and is recovered by niche energy routing (67.3%); task-free discovery reaches 96.65% purity under strong contrast and fails in a measured way without it. Both papers follow the same golden rule: no claim without an experiment behind it, and no number that does not survive the authors' own bad faith. Negative and refuted results are reported alongside the positive ones. Licensing: source code is MIT; the papers and written material are CC BY 4.0 (see LICENSE and LICENSE-PAPERS.md).

title: WirelessOpsAgent: A Benchmark and Agent Design for Action Assurance in Wireless Networks
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are emerging as planners for autonomous wireless network operations. Yet a task answer that is correct at proposal time can still be unsafe at execution time if supporting telemetry is stale or inconsistent. Existing benchmarks mainly evaluate task solving from fixed observations and leave support checking at execution time untested. We introduce WirelessOptBench, a benchmark for action assurance in wireless operations. It turns wireless tasks into execution state decision episodes with controlled telemetry faults and action constraints. We further develop WirelessOpsAgent, which grounds candidate actions in current evidence and repairs recoverable support failures before execution. Across three backbone evaluations with 600 episodes each, WirelessOpsAgent achieves up to 0.983 Exact Action Accuracy. On Claude Sonnet 4.6, the Unsafe APPLY Rate decreases from 82.2% to 10.3% relative to the safest baseline. We make WirelessOptBench available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/wirelessopsbench-artifact-D969/.

title: Sarcasm Detection Using Learning Techniques in a Social Engineering Context: A PRISMA-Based Systematic Review
abstract: Sarcasm—the deliberate expression of a meaning opposite to the literal content of an utterance—is pervasive in social-media communication and constitutes a major source of error for sentiment analysis, opinion mining and manipulation-detection systems deployed in social-engineering contexts. Because sarcasm inverts surface polarity, its automatic detection remains a hard, context-dependent natural-language-processing (NLP) problem. This paper presents a systematic review conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Eight bibliographic databases were searched for the period 2010–2026; from 1,320 identified records, a four-phase identification–screening–eligibility–inclusion process yielded 40 primary studies for synthesis. Beyond the review protocol, the paper provides an extended theoretical foundation covering pragmatic theories of irony, text representation, classical machine-learning classifiers, recurrent and convolutional architectures, the attention and Transformer formalism, pre-trained language models, multimodal fusion and evaluation metrics. The synthesis is organised around four research questions addressing (RQ1) benchmark datasets and social-media text sources, (RQ2) NLP pre-processing techniques, (RQ3) machine-learning and deep-learning models, and (RQ4) transformer-based and context-aware models, with a dedicated comparison at each question and a per-study questionnaire-style extraction form. Results reveal a clear methodological progression from feature-engineered classifiers, through CNN/RNN and attention hybrids, to transformer and multimodal graph architectures, with contextual embeddings consistently improving performance. Persistent gaps include weak modelling of extra-utterance context, noisy distant-supervision labels, severe class imbalance in intended-sarcasm corpora, limited cross-domain and code-mixed generalisation, and poor interpretability. On this basis we outline a precision-aware, context-integrating sarcasm-prediction algorithm and an evaluation protocol for validation against the state of the art.

title: The Chameleon Neuron: Emergent Retention, Transmutation, and Abstention in a Continual-Learning Organism
abstract: We present the Chameleon Neuron, a continual-learning organism whose unit is a low-rankstem neuron with epigenetic marks and a context meta-selector, organized as a dynamicpopulation that grows by neurogenesis, specializes into niches, and consolidates offline.Rather than treating forgetting, domain adaptation and out-of-distribution (OOD) detectionas separate problems, we show that three capabilities coexist on one substrate, withoutbinary masks and without replay: retention (not forgetting), transmutation (classifyingknown-but-corrupted inputs), and abstention (rejecting true OOD). We validate onSplit-CIFAR-100 over frozen ResNet-18 features (5 seeds) and, unusually, audit our ownclaims adversarially, reporting what survives and what does not. We do not claim per-axissupremacy: retention matches PackNet at the reported size (BWT -0.00 +/- 0.16%, 85.10 +/-0.43%), but at matched parameters PackNet and EWC pull ahead, and a learned L2P-stylerouter beats our task-free routing (55.8% vs 38.6% Class-IL) with 1/26 of the parameters.One robustness result turns a principle into a method: signal decoupling. A decoupledlearned gate combining distance and energy is the only detector strong on both far- andnear-OOD (0.99 far, 0.83 SVHN), where distance collapses on near-OOD and energy is weak onfar-OOD; the contribution is insurance against regime collapse, not an accuracy win. Theaudit methodology is itself a contribution: it exposed and made us fix an abstention gatecalibrated on the test set, and routing inflated by homogeneous batches plus an EMA-scalebug (honest per-sample routing 36% -> 44.6%). Every number that survived bad faith isreported as such; every one that did not, we fixed or retired.

title: Self-Healing Containment Graphs: Trusted Reconstruction After Transitive Contamination
abstract: Correct transitive containment can disable far more legitimate state than an attacker directly compromised. CSR-PUB-0002 defined and measured that effect as containment denial of service (CDoS); CSR-PUB-0003 showed that operational availability can be restored by adding replacement capacity without weakening the containment footprint, while returning a negative decision on its own preregistered joint rule. Both leave the quarantined state itself permanently unavailable. This paper asks whether trusted usable state can be _reconstructed_ after correct containment — without clearing taint, without reducing historical quarantine, without reusing a contaminated identity, and without consulting hidden material truth. We specify a governed repair mechanism in which repaired state is emitted forward under a new identity with fresh provenance rather than restored in place: an admissible frontier is computed from runtime-visible state only, a planner selects an authorized reconstruction method, a verifier re-derives the candidate and rejects on disagreement rather than tie-breaking, a graph-safety gate blocks any admission that would reintroduce prohibited ancestry into the active graph, and a bounded recurrence monitor withdraws admitted state if contamination reappears — without erasing the original decision. Every decision is bound to its inputs by digest. The confirmatory design is a fully paired campaign over the frozen CSR-BENCH-1.0 population: 2,331 base cells per seed × (7 profiles × 9 recovery challenges + 4 negative controls), 30 confirmatory seeds, 4,685,310 trials. Across 4,685,176 materialized trials, governed repair raises verified repair coverage over continuity alone by a median paired difference of +0.600 (probability of superiority 1.000, Holm-adjusted p = 0.0007), and it does so without weakening containment: over 69,928 matched cells the historical quarantine digest is identical, the paired CPI, WCAL and recovery-eligible-record differences are exactly zero, and the counts of taint clears, quarantine reductions, identity reuses, hidden-truth uses, verifier bypasses, incomplete-provenance admissions and prohibited-ancestry admissions are all zero, while every isolated unsafe control records its own distinct violation. The remaining parents do not clear their frozen bars: H2 is inconclusive because 89% of its pairs are incomplete, H3 and H4 each fail a required sub-comparison (one of which has no eligible pairs at all), H5 fails because the frozen median trusted-function-restoration difference is zero, H6 fails a different clause — governed recurrence exceeds single-mechanism substitute reconstruction by more than its 0.005 non-inferiority margin, even though governed repair beats all three single mechanisms on coverage — and H7 is unevaluable because the preregistered high-burden label saturates to a single class. The preregistered joint success rule is therefore not satisfied, and roughly 39% of governed repair targets are irreducible by construction. The scope was fixed in advance and is unchanged by the outcome: a bounded existence-and-direction finding inside a synthetic benchmark, not evidence that any product self-heals a deployed system.

title: Named Entity Recognition
abstract: Named Entity Recognition (NER) is the task of identifying and categorizing references to entities — such as persons, organizations, places, or events — within text (Jehangir et al., 2023). State-of-the-art NER models are usually transformer-based (Balluff et al., 2024), though rule-based, unsupervised, and more recently Large Language Model-based approaches are also in use. In the social sciences, NER is commonly applied as a pre-processing step, for instance to study the salience or sentiment of actors in media coverage. Field of Application/Theoretical Foundation Named Entity Recognition is the “task of recognizing and categorizing named entities that are presented in a text document” (Jehangir et al., 2023, p. 1), where anything denotable by a proper name can count as a named entity (Jurafsky & Martin, 2026, p. 387). In the social sciences, named entities are often actors broadly defined: individual persons as well as collective actors such as political parties or social movements (Schwarz, 2025), but also events (e.g., “Swiss national election 2023”), legal constructs (e.g., “EU AI Act”), or infrastructure projects (e.g., “Nord Stream”) (Balluff et al., 2024). NER is generally regarded as a pre-processing technique (Munnangi, 2024) useful for many social science applications. Common applications in communication research include studying the salience of actors in media coverage (Ort et al., 2023; Wozniak et al., 2026; Zai et al., 2025) or actor visibility on social media (Kruikemeier et al., 2018). To identify entities, there exists a plethora of NER approaches that can be categorized in many ways. Seow et al. (2025) provide the most recent and most comprehensive review. We use a broad categorization for the purpose of this entry. First, rule-based NER approaches use a carefully designed collection of rules to identify entities by relying on tailored dictionaries or sets of task-specific heuristics (Seow et al., 2025). This approach works well for narrow, well-defined tasks, such as identifying specific politicians in text (e.g., Gattermann, 2018). However, rule-based approaches don’t generalize well across languages or domains or even research questions (Jehangir et al., 2023). Second, unsupervised approaches rely on techniques that identify entities without labeled data (Jehangir et al., 2023). Computer science research has developed such approaches (e.g., Iovine et al., 2022; Zhang & Elhadad, 2013), whereby the model learns to identify entities from the data alone. One common application is the detection of drug names in biomedical sciences (Zhang & Elhadad, 2013), yet such approaches are rarely used in the social sciences. Unsupervised approaches are versatile and don’t require labeled data. However, their biggest difficulty is that their application typically lacks a ground truth (“gold standard”), which makes validation difficult (Seow et al., 2025). Third, supervised approaches rely on labeled data to classify entities. Typical applications use feature extraction methods such as part-of-speech tagging and subsequently learn these patterns using machine learning algorithms (Munnangi, 2024). A variety of algorithms can be used, ranging from more classical models like Hidden Markov models (Zhou & Su, 2002) to deep learning models (Jehangir et al., 2023). More recently, transfer learning approaches have gained traction. Balluff et al. (2024) find that these transformer-based approaches perform best on social science applications. Models trained in a supervised manner are sometimes applied in different contexts without additional labeled data. A common ready-to-use pipeline is the spaCy text processing toolkit for Python or R (Honnibal et al., 2020). Fourth, computer science literature has developed NER approaches that use a Large Language Model (LLM) with zero-shot or few-shot learning, where the LLM is prompted to identify and categorize entities without examples (zero-shot) or with a small number of examples (few-shot) (e.g., Wang et al., 2025; Zhu & Liu, 2025). However, existing tools still face several shortcomings: most are optimized for English text and specific domains, and they generally cannot disambiguate entities that share the same surface form (e.g., two different people both named "John Smith") without an additional entity-linking step (Schwarz, 2025). Of note, the literature on natural language processing treats this last step as a different but related problem called Named Entity Disambiguation (Al-Moslmi et al., 2020). References / Combination with other Methods Because NER is a pre-processing technique (Munnangi, 2024), it rarely stands alone. Often, the extracted entities are subsequently used in combination with other methods. The output of NER can be used to measure similarity between texts through shared named entities, for example to study news influence (Welbers et al., 2018) or news story chains (Gedikli et al., 2021). In a similar vein, co-occurring entities within documents can be used to construct networks of actors (Traag et al., 2015). With such an approach networks of political elites can be constructed from news coverage (e.g., Bro, 2025). Other applications use NER to analyze targeted sentiment towards actors (e.g., Fogel-Dror et al., 2019). Example Studies To illustrate how the rule-based, unsupervised, supervised, and LLM-based approaches discussed above translate into applied social science research, the table below compares four studies that differ in scope, entity taxonomy, and language, but together span this continuum (Licht & Sczepanski, 2025; Nenno, 2025; Ort et al., 2023; Zaratiana et al., 2023). Three of the four studies develop and validate a custom NER approach; the fourth illustrates the common case in which NER is used as an off-the-shelf pre-processing step rather than as the object of methodological evaluation. Table 1: Comparison of Named Entity Recognition approaches. Article Approach Entity types/domain Language(s) Validation/performance Nenno (2025) Domain-specific supervised NER via continuous fine-tuning (CFT): a transformer (XLM-R) first fine-tuned on weakly labeled data (dictionary matching against a database of public speakers), then further fine-tuned on a small manually annotated set 5 custom categories specific to public discourse: politicians, parties, authorities, media, journalists ("Public Entity Recognition") German (training); adapted to English and Spanish Outperforms the rule-based dictionary baseline (F1 .37–.61) by a wide margin, reaching F1 ≈ .8 on in-domain, out-of-domain, and Twitter data; with only ~100–150 additional labeled sentences, performance on English/Spanish improves from ≈ .6 (zero-shot) to ≈ .8 Licht & Sczepanski (2025) Supervised token classification (BIO-tagging) by fine-tuning transformer encoders (DeBERTa/RoBERTa) on human-annotated word spans Broadly defined "social group mentions" in political rhetoric (e.g., workers, refugees, "ordinary working people") English (UK party manifestos, parliamentary speech); cross-lingual transfer tested on German Mention-level F1 = .87 (cross-validated); document-level counts correlate strongly with an independent manual content analysis (Thau, 2019; r = .94); reliable few-shot transfer to new parties, domains, and languages with a few hundred additional labeled sentences Zaratiana et al. (2023) Generalist zero-/few-shot NER: a small bidirectional transformer matches entity-type embeddings to text-span embeddings, avoiding costly autoregressive LLM prompting Open/arbitrary entity types, specified in natural language at inference time rather than fixed in advance Trained on English data; generalizes zero-shot to several other languages Outperforms ChatGPT and several fine-tuned LLMs (e.g., UniNER) on zero-shot out-of-domain NER benchmarks, despite being orders of magnitude smaller (a 50M-parameter version still beats multi-billion-parameter models) Ort et al. (2023) Off-the-shelf NER (spaCy) applied without custom training, followed by manual classification of the most frequent entities into broader actor categories General-purpose entities (persons, organizations, places), grouped post hoc into four societal actor types (politics, government, economy, science) German and French (Swiss news coverage) No dedicated NER validation reported; relies on spaCy's established benchmark performance plus a manual face-validity check of the 150 most frequent entities; NER serves purely as a pre-processing step feeding into a downstream statistical analysis References Al-Moslmi, T., Gallofré Ocaña, M., Opdahl, A. Common applications in communication research include studying the salience of actors in media coverage (Ort et al., 2023; Wozniak et al., 2026; Zai et al., 2025) or actor visibility on social media (Kruikemeier et al., 2018). To identify entities, there exists a plethora of NER approaches that can be categorized in many ways. Seow et al. (2025) provide the most recent and most comprehensive review. We use a broad categorization for the purpose of this entry. First, rule-based NER approaches use a carefully designed collection of rules to identify entities by relying on tailored dictionaries or sets of task-specific heuristics (Seow et al., 2025). This approach works well for narrow, well-defined tasks, such as identifying specific politicians in text (e.g., Gattermann, 2018). However, rule-based approaches don’t generalize well across languages or domains or even research questions (Jehangir et al., 2023). Second, unsupervised approaches rely on techniques that identify entities without labeled data (Jehangir et al., 2023). Computer science research has developed such approaches (e.g., Iovine et al., 2022; Zhang & Elhadad, 2013), whereby the model learns to identify entities from the data alone. One common application is the detection of drug names in biomedical sciences (Zhang & Elhadad, 2013), yet such approaches are rarely used in the social sciences. Unsupervised approaches are versatile and don’t require labeled data. However, their biggest difficulty is that their application typically lacks a ground truth (“gold standard”), which makes validation difficult (Seow et al., 2025). Third, supervised approaches rely on labeled data to classify entities. Typical applications use feature extraction methods such as part-of-speech tagging and subsequently learn these patterns using machine learning algorithms (Munnangi, 2024). A variety of algorithms can be used, ranging from more classical models like Hidden Markov models (Zhou & Su, 2002) to deep learning models (Jehangir et al., 2023). More recently, transfer learning approaches have gained traction. Balluff et al. (2024) find that these transformer-based approaches perform best on social science applications. Models trained in a supervised manner are sometimes applied in different contexts without additional labeled data. A common ready-to-use pipeline is the spaCy text processing toolkit for Python or R (Honnibal et al., 2020). Fourth, computer science literature has developed NER approaches that use a Large Language Model (LLM) with zero-shot or few-shot learning, where the LLM is prompted to identify and categorize entities without examples (zero-shot) or with a small number of examples (few-shot) (e.g., Wang et al., 2025; Zhu & Liu, 2025). However, existing tools still face several shortcomings: most are optimized for English text and specific domains, and they generally cannot disambiguate entities that share the same surface form (e.g., two different people both named "John Smith") without an additional entity-linking step (Schwarz, 2025). Of note, the literature on natural language processing treats this last step as a different but related problem called Named Entity Disambiguation (Al-Moslmi et al., 2020). References / Combination with other Methods Because NER is a pre-processing technique (Munnangi, 2024), it rarely stands alone. Often, the extracted entities are subsequently used in combination with other methods. The output of NER can be used to measure similarity between texts through shared named entities, for example to study news influence (Welbers et al., 2018) or news story chains (Gedikli et al., 2021). In a similar vein, co-occurring entities within documents can be used to construct networks of actors (Traag et al., 2015). With such an approach networks of political elites can be constructed from news coverage (e.g., Bro, 2025). Other applications use NER to analyze targeted sentiment towards actors (e.g., Fogel-Dror et al., 2019). Example Studies To illustrate how the rule-based, unsupervised, supervised, and LLM-based approaches discussed above translate into applied social science research, the table below compares four studies that differ in scope, entity taxonomy, and language, but together span this continuum (Licht & Sczepanski, 2025; Nenno, 2025; Ort et al., 2023; Zaratiana et al., 2023). Three of the four studies develop and validate a custom NER approach; the fourth illustrates the common case in which NER is used as an off-the-shelf pre-processing step rather than as the object of methodological evaluation. title: Gendered Adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence among Gen Z Social Media Influencers in Malaysia’s Content Creation Industry: Intellectual Property Challenges and Ethical Imperatives
abstract: This conceptual review examines gender differences in the adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) by Generation Z (Gen Z) social media influencers and content creators operating online businesses in Malaysia. Drawing on recent empirical and policy evidence from 2025–2026, it analyses how male and female Gen Z creators differentially integrate AI tools into content production, audience engagement, and monetisation strategies within Malaysia’s rapidly expanding creator economy and high social-media penetration environment (Telenor Asia, 2025). Parallel attention is given to emerging intellectual property (IP) ambiguities surrounding AI-assisted and AI-generated content, alongside ethical concerns including authenticity, disclosure obligations, deepfake risks, cultural representation, and algorithmic bias. Findings synthesised from contemporary studies indicate functional differentiation rather than simple access gaps: male creators more frequently employ AI for technical and coding-oriented tasks, while female creators concentrate on text generation, creative writing, and aesthetic enhancement (Raza et al., 2026). Persistent gendered risk perceptions regarding societal harms further moderate adoption intensity, particularly among younger women (Stephany & Duszynski, 2026). Malaysia’s human-centred copyright framework under the Copyright Act 1987 leaves significant gaps for AI-generated works, exposing creators, especially those building personal brands, to ownership uncertainty and unauthorised replication of likeness or style (Wardi et al., 2025). The paper proposes an integrated ethical-governance and IP-reform agenda tailored to the Malaysian creator ecosystem and calls for gender-responsive AI literacy programmes, mandatory disclosure standards, and updated guidance from the Malaysian Intellectual Property Organisation (MyIPO). Implications for policy, platform design, and future empirical research are discussed.

title: Neurosymbolic Discovery of Algebraic Graph Constructions: Supplementary Material (NeSy 2026)
abstract: Software and experimental data backing each empirical claim in: David Seka and Stefan Szeider, "Neurosymbolic Discovery of Algebraic Graph Constructions", NeSy 2026 (20th International Conference on Neurosymbolic Learning and Reasoning), PMLR vol. 284. The archive contains: the pre-registered 100-graph benchmark of two-orbit graphs (graph6 targets and metadata); all agent run transcripts (100 capability runs, a 40-graph backbone pre-study across five models, a 50-graph symmetry-stratified reliability set, a 20-graph planted-construction recall test, and the Bernhart-Kainen case study); the verbatim system prompt and grading prompt; the two non-LLM baselines (strong template enumeration and literature lookup) with scripts and results; per-run isomorphism verification and LLM-judge grades; a human-audit package for judge calibration; and archival copies of the two released software tools. Replay instructions are in README.md (uvx mcp-minion@0.2.1; requires SageMath 10.6+ and an OpenRouter API key). The two bundled software folders are MIT-licensed, Copyright (c) 2026 Stefan Szeider, and are maintained outside this archive: mcp-sage, the SageMath MCP server (https://github.com/szeider/mcp-sage, PyPI: mcp-sage), and mcp-minion, the ReAct agent harness (https://github.com/szeider/mcp-solver, PyPI: mcp-minion). All other content is licensed CC BY 4.0.

title: Meridian Affinity Calculus (MAC) v4.4 Ordered Projection Architecture: An Exploratory Research Framework for Temporal Organization, Influence, and Residual Structure
abstract: MERIDIAN AFFINITY CALCULUS (MAC) v4.4 THE LIVING RESIDUAL LABORATORY Ordered Projection, Temporal Organization, Influence, and Information Survival in Complex Systems AI / ML / LLM Research Extension · 2026 Published: 11 August 2026 · Version: v4 / v4.4 framework Status: Independent Research Framework / Exploratory Mathematical Architecture / Working Paper Author: E.J. Vening FROM ORDERING TO RESIDUALS Meridian Affinity Calculus (MAC) is an exploratory research framework for investigating whether measurable organizational structure can remain after conventional explanations, transformations, and representations have been accounted for. The central question is deliberately narrower than a theory of everything: After known effects have been modelled, controlled, or removed, what structure remains? MAC investigates whether that remaining structure can be associated with temporal organization, persistence, affinity, sequential history, projection constraints, or other measurable properties of a system. It does not introduce a new fundamental force. It does not assume that an unexplained residual represents a new phenomenon. It does not replace established physical, statistical, computational, or biological models. Instead, MAC provides an intermediate experimental architecture in which candidate residual structures can be measured, challenged, reproduced, rejected, or retained as unresolved. THE LIVING RESIDUAL LABORATORY The 2026 extension develops MAC into a practical laboratory for studying information survival through transformation. Rather than evaluating an intelligent system only by its final answer, the Living Residual Laboratory asks what happens to the structure that existed before the answer. That structure may include: goals; constraints; relationships; ordering information; historical dependencies; organisational patterns; context; decision trajectories; intermediate states; unresolved information. The laboratory therefore investigates a broader question: How much of an information structure survives processing, compression, retrieval, transformation, and reasoning? This provides a possible experimental language for studying AI memory, conversational continuity, agent trajectories, retrieval systems, summarization, sequential decision-making, and other systems in which information changes state over time. THE RESEARCH TRANSITION ORDER | v TEMPORAL ORGANIZATION | v PROJECTION | v TRANSFORMATION | v RESIDUAL | v MEASUREMENT | v CHALLENGE | v VALIDATION / REJECTION / UNRESOLVED The Living Residual Laboratory adds an explicit experimental layer to this progression. Instead of asking only whether a system produces the expected output, it permits investigation of what information survives the journey to that output. CORE RESEARCH QUESTION MAC asks whether statistically or informationally significant residual structure can remain after known physical, geometric, environmental, statistical, and computational contributions have been accounted for. The question is strictly empirical. The strongest null is intentionally severe: ABSOLUTE NULL:No recoverable ordering information exists beyond ordinary state variables and known effects. Any proposed ordering effect must therefore survive attempts to explain it through conventional mechanisms. CORE MAC CONCEPTS Concept Function within the framework Affinity Structure Relational compatibility and influence between components, considered across local, distant, and remote regimes. Organisational Compression Retention of historically relevant structure rather than complete microscopic state preservation. SIEVE Multi-factor filtering and ranking of candidate structures according to persistence, coherence, information contribution, alternatives, and temporal organization. Sequential Projection Ordering (SPO) A proposed mechanism for investigating how available influences become ordered into an expressed state. Order Residual ΔO The measurable difference between appropriately matched systems whose controlled difference lies in temporal or organisational history. Coherency Ruler The measurement frame defining which relational structure becomes observable within a particular analysis. THE SIEVE PRINCIPLE SIEVE is not intended to manufacture certainty. It is a mechanism for preventing candidate structure from being promoted prematurely. CANDIDATE STRUCTURE | v PERSISTENCE | v COHERENCE | v INFORMATION CONTRIBUTION | v ALTERNATIVE RESISTANCE | v TEMPORAL ORGANIZATION | +---------> REJECT | +---------> UNRESOLVED | +---------> RETAIN / ADMIT FOR FURTHER TESTING The distinction is fundamental: retention is not confirmation. RESEARCH PRINCIPLES No unsupported ontology. Every additional coordinate, variable, or structural concept must improve prediction, measurement, discrimination, or reproducibility — otherwise it should remain provisional or be removed. Explicit failure conditions. Every hypothesis should have a meaningful null test and identifiable conditions under which it fails. Known effects first. Conventional explanations should be modelled or controlled before unexplained residuals are attributed to ordering or organisational history. Reproducibility. Measurements should be independently repeatable wherever the data and computational environment permit. Provisional status. A residual remains a residual until evidence justifies a stronger interpretation. THE AI / ML / LLM EXTENSION The Living Residual Laboratory opens MAC to a particularly difficult class of sequential systems: artificial intelligence. Modern AI systems do not merely transform isolated inputs into isolated outputs. They retrieve, compress, summarize, rank, reinterpret, predict, revise, and regenerate information across increasingly long interaction histories. This creates an experimentally accessible question: When an AI system transforms information, what survives? The proposed AI/ML research direction therefore shifts attention from output accuracy alone toward information continuity. AI RESEARCH DIRECTIONS Context Fidelity Diagnostics Measure whether goals, constraints, important facts, relationships, and task requirements remain represented faithfully as an interaction progresses. AI Residual Analysis Investigate structural information that remains after conventional explanatory effects have been accounted for. Conversational Residuals Treat long-running AI interactions as evolving sequential information structures rather than merely collections of independent prompts and answers. Memory Architecture Evaluation Provide experimental pathways for comparing summarization, retrieval, episodic memory, persistent context, and other approaches to maintaining information over time. Organisational Preservation Measure whether relationships and structures survive even when literal wording, token sequences, or surface representations change. FROM GENERATING ANSWERS TO PRESERVING STRUCTURE A conventional evaluation might ask: Did the system produce the correct answer? The Living Residual Laboratory adds another question: What happened to the information required to produce that answer? And another: What information was lost, transformed, compressed, reconstructed, or unexpectedly preserved? This does not replace conventional accuracy testing. It adds another dimension. THE CONVERSATIONAL TRAJECTORY AS AN OBJECT OF STUDY An extended AI interaction can be represented conceptually as a sequence: S0 → S1 → S2 → S3 → ... → Sn where each transition may involve: CONTEXT ↓ RETRIEVAL ↓ TRANSFORMATION ↓ REASONING ↓ COMPRESSION ↓ RECONSTRUCTION ↓ OUTPUT MAC asks whether the trajectory itself contains measurable structure that cannot be adequately described by the final state alone. This opens experimental comparisons between: ordinary progressive summarization; retrieval-based memory; anchor-preserving compression; history-aware reasoning; context-window reconstruction; agentic tool trajectories; independent repeated runs. THE CONVENTIONAL-EFFECT FILTER BANK The operational extension adds conventional statistical tools before residual interpretation. Method Purpose ARIMA / SARIMA Temporal structure and predictable components GARCH-family models Conditional variance and volatility structure EWMA standardisation Adaptive scale normalization Fractional differencing Long-memory-aware transformation Rank correlations Monotonic relational structure Pearson correlation Linear association Rolling analysis Temporal stability and regime changes Pivot statistics Changes around identified structural transitions The purpose of this filter bank is not to guarantee that every conventional effect has been removed. It is to make the removal process explicit, inspectable, and reproducible. SYMMETRY AND MULTI-METRIC TESTING Residual claims should not depend on a single statistic. The operational laboratory therefore supports multiple complementary measures, including: L1-based comparisons; Kendall τ; Spearman correlation; Pearson correlation; rolling-window relationships; pivot-change statistics; trajectory-level comparisons. Agreement across metrics is not automatically evidence of independence. It is an opportunity to test whether a result survives different measurement formulations. LLM-AUGMENTED EXPERIMENTATION The LLM is treated as an experimental assistant rather than as an epistemic authority. A proposed automated loop is: DATA ↓ CONVENTIONAL FILTERING ↓ RESIDUAL EXTRACTION ↓ MULTI-METRIC ANALYSIS ↓ LLM INTERPRETATION ↓ ALTERNATIVE HYPOTHESES ↓ NEXT FALSIFICATION TEST ↓ EXECUTION ↓ EVIDENCE ↓ REVISED QUESTION The LLM can propose interpretations, identify possible

title: Walking on thin ice? Defending RAG-based code recommender systems against poisoning attacks
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been extensively adopted in software engineering to automate various tasks, including code comment generation, debugging, testing, and most notably, code generation. Retrieval-Augmented Code Generation (RACG) further enhances LLMs by incorporating external code repositories at inference time, but this design also introduces a new system-level security risk: knowledge-base poisoning, where adversarial or vulnerable code is injected into the retrieval corpus to steer generation toward insecure implementations. In this paper, we address the problem of defending RACG system against poisoning attacks by proposing RAGGuard , a defense-oriented framework that explicitly accounts for the presence of untrusted retrieved code exemplars during code generation. Rather than assuming benign retrievals, RAGGuard introduces system-level defense mechanisms that mitigate vulnerabilities induced by poisoned exemplars in the retrieval-generation pipeline. RAGGuard is developed atop LLM-based agents with three defense strategies: (i) Establishing a self-verifying workflow to autonomously assess and iteratively refine generated code for security under poisoned retrieval code exemplars; (ii) Leveraging security warnings to identify vulnerabilities embedded in retrieved code and prevent their propagation into generated outputs; and (iii) Embedding standardized vulnerability knowledge to guide secure code refinement and reduce sensitivity to instance-level poisoning. We evaluate RAGGuard through an empirical study involving five LLMs, and the results show that RAGGuard outperforms the baselines and enhances code security, with the third strategy achieving substantial secure-rate improvements, while preserving functional correctness. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of system-level defense mechanisms in mitigating retrieval-induced security risks in RAG-based code generation systems.

title: Refined^2 Environment Classifiers
abstract: MetaML-style multi-stage programming (MSP) supports quasi-quotation-based code generation, runtime execution of generated code, and cross-stage persistence (CSP). However, its interaction with computational effects is subtle: mutable state can cause scope extrusion, where generated code escapes the scope of variables on which it depends. This paper presents a type system for MetaML-style MSP with mutable state that statically rules out harmful scope extrusion while supporting multi-level code generation, runtime execution, and a variant of CSP. Our system builds on refined environment classifiers (RECs), a discipline that annotates code types with the variable scopes on which generated code depends. To scale RECs to the MetaML-style setting, we refine classifiers so that they track not only variable scopes, but also the scopes of classifiers themselves. Further, we integrated polymorphism over classifiers, enabling more general and reusable code generation patterns in a multi-level setting. For the resulting system, we define an operational semantics via a definitional interpreter and prove type soundness and safety of offline code generation, showing that generated code can be extracted as standalone well-typed programs. We provide working implementations and mechanized proofs in Rocq.

title: Why Tactic-Level Rates Cannot Attribute Classical Dependencies in Lean
abstract: A proof assistant reports which axioms a theorem depends on. It does not report which step introduced them, and a proof invoking several tactics offers no way to apportion the answer. The obvious approach is statistical: score each tactic by how often its proofs carry a classical dependence the theorem did not require, and rank them. This paper reports that the approach cannot work, and gives the reason. The reason is a mismatch of random variables. Eligibility - a proof reaching Classical.choice where the statement does not - is a property of the theorem. Whether a tactic introduced that dependence is a property of the proof term. A rate conditioned on the first cannot recover the second, and the measurements show it does not. Calibration is by known-negatives: tactics that cannot introduce a classical instance, whose rate is therefore background. Across the four Lean libraries containing enough hand-written tactic proofs to measure them, that background is neither small nor constant. In Mathlib it spans 5.8 to 28.2 per cent across 30 known-negatives; in Lean core 45.0 to 100.0 per cent, with trivial at the top. rfl, which cannot introduce a classical instance, scores 16.2 per cent in Mathlib, 28.0 in Std, 48.7 in Batteries and 65.6 in Lean core. The variation is as large within a library as between them, so no normalisation recovers a threshold. Against those bands, seven candidate escapes occur across four libraries and two controls. Four belong to grind, which is not defective: it proves by refuting the negation, and refutation is classical by construction. One belongs to omega, whose classical dependence is an uncontested measurement, and simp_all ties it at exactly 100.0 per cent in the same cell. None belongs to norm_num, which sits at 5.0 per cent in Mathlib, below the known-negative floor, beneath rfl and exfalso. That last is the paper's positive result, obtained by a different method. Controlled differential construction - posing the same goal to a tactic and its alternatives and comparing axiom sets - establishes that norm_num closes numeric order goals over the naturals and integers through Classical.choice where decide and simp close them without it, by routing through a general PartialOrder lemma on types that carry DecidableEq. Equality goals are unaffected. It is a real, avoidable dependence that every rate in this paper ranks below background. A third result bounds the ambition. interval_cases scores at the top of its corpus and is innocent: its proofs close with a combinator handing the goal to norm_num, and it carries norm_num's dependence. Attribution to a surface tactic is the wrong unit regardless of the statistic. True attribution is a term-level problem, and is not solved here. Measurements cover 532,605 Mathlib theorems, three further Lean libraries, and 9,169 machine-generated proofs from the Goedel-Prover corpus. All figures derive from a single pipeline with one join rule; the accompanying archive reproduces the corpus figures with one command and no Lean, corpus download or network access.

title: Training Dataset for the Name Spell Model
abstract: This repo contains five (5) datasets used for training, validating and testing the Name Spell Model hosted on Hugging Face. Each CSV file contains Hausa personal names and their corresponding spelling attempts, which are a combination of real and synthetic data. The experiment involved fine-tuning ByT5 small, Flan-T5 small and AfroLlaMA for the purpose of predicting the correct spelling of misspelt Hausa Personal names. The base and corresponding fine-tuned models were evaluated, and their predictions are provided in the respective CSV files attached herein.

title: Impact of Intermediate Task Difficulty on Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Transfer Performance in XTREME-R
abstract: Intermediate-task training---fine-tuning a pretrained model on an intermediate task before fine-tuning again on the target task---often improves model performance substantially on language understanding tasks in monolingual English settings. We investigate whether English intermediate-task training is still helpful on non-English target tasks. Using nine intermediate language-understanding tasks, we evaluate intermediate-task transfer in a zero-shot cross-lingual setting on the XTREME benchmark. We see large improvements from intermediate training on the BUCC and Tatoeba sentence retrieval tas Research goal: How does the selection of intermediate task difficulty (e.g., easy vs. hard language understanding tasks) impact zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance on the XTREME-R benchmark compared to random task selection? title: Relational Search Operator Specification 0.1: Frozen Method, Validation Record, and Prospective Test Protocol
abstract: Relational Search Operator Specification 0.1 is the first frozen normative checkpoint of an explicit reasoning/search procedure for organizing evidence around scoped relations, witnessed boundary crossings, materially different candidate structures, consequence and residue, contradiction and valid absence, rejection conditions, and best-next-question handoff. The release preserves the operator together with its pre-freeze validation record, authorised claims and limitations, provenance, evidence index, frozen comparative results, and a prospective blind Human vs Strong Baseline vs Relational Search vs external-reality test protocol that had not yet been run when version 0.1 was frozen. Across the pre-freeze benchmarks, Relational Search showed robust and calibrated handling of functional, temporal, identity, provenance, contradiction, resolution, authority, causal, and correlation-only cases. Direct controlled comparisons did not demonstrate material superiority over a strongest general analytical baseline: CP1 and CP2 were primary-score ties; CP3 is retained as a confounded comparison because its baseline instructions were inadvertently relationally primed; and CP4 was a valid clean 20/20 versus 20/20 tie. The release therefore presents Relational Search as an explicit and recoverable reasoning/audit architecture, not as a demonstrated superior-intelligence or automatic-discovery system. This public freeze is intended to make subsequent validation prospective and auditable. Future successful applications, proofs, experiments, or domain discoveries retain their own discovery credit; they should not be attributed to this specification merely because the method helped formulate a useful question or relation.

title: Fault diagnostics in intelligent control systems of autonomous robots: An ontological approach
abstract: Objectives. The work set out to develop diagnostic tools and methods for autonomous robots for the rapid detection of faults based on the analysis of cause-and-effect relationships between observed manifestations and the sources of failures. Methods. The paper presents an analytical review of the current scientific and technical literature on the topic of the research, which includes ontology construction methods for developing a diagnostic model for autonomous robots, Boolean algebra methods for generating queries to the ontological diagnostic model, modifications to conditional and unconditional diagnostic methods for finding cause-and-effect relationships between failures and malfunctions based on the use of an ontological model, and machine experimentation methods for estimating the processing time of queries to the ontological diagnostic model. Results. The presented ontological model and methods for conditional and unconditional diagnostics is used to establish cause-and-effect relationships between observed failures and the malfunctions that cause them. Conclusions. Based on an ontological approach and taking into account the availability of advanced tool support, including ontology description languages, ontology modeling tools, and ontology-based inference and reasoning technologies, a new paradigm is identified for the development of a promising class of autonomous robotic systems with increased fault tolerance and, consequently, adaptability. The development of an autonomous robot presupposes the presence of an onboard intelligent control system built on a hierarchical principle that comprises executive, tactical, and strategic levels. The results of the ontological model provide an effective basis for activating and utilizing the intelligent control system’s rich algorithm databases at all levels of the control hierarchy to support increased adaptability.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Pharmaceutical Commercial Leadership: A Practical Framework for Building High-Performance Commercial Organizations
abstract: This White Paper examines how Artificial Intelligence is reshaping pharmaceutical commercial leadership, arguing that AI strengthens leadership by extending managerial judgment, pattern recognition, and decision support; it is not a substitute for the leader. Drawing on more than two decades of the author's experience managing multinational pharmaceutical field organizations, together with established leadership and management literature, the paper traces the historical evolution of pharmaceutical commercial organizations through four eras and proposes two original conceptual models: the Kavun Adaptive Commercial Leadership Framework™ (KACL) and the Field Force Operating System™ (FFOS). These models describe how human leadership, organizational intelligence, and Artificial Intelligence can be integrated to support predictive decision-making, adaptive territory management, AI-assisted leadership coaching, and continuous organizational learning within pharmaceutical commercial operations. The paper further discusses practical implementation phases, common transformation failures, and the anticipated evolution of Medical Representative, Regional Manager, and Field Force Manager roles toward 2035. As a conceptual and practitioner-oriented contribution rather than an empirical study, the paper concludes by acknowledging its limitations and proposing directions for future empirical and interdisciplinary research on AI-augmented commercial leadership in the pharmaceutical industry.

abstract: Trained model checkpoints for the MSc dissertation "Mitigating Temporal Drift in Social Media Sentiment Classification: A Comparative Study" (Queen Mary University of London, MSc Artificial Intelligence). title: A Machine Learning framework for explainable clinical diagnosis using health records
abstract: The integration of large datasets in healthcare, particularly through Electronic Health Records (EHR), has enabled critical insights into patient care and treatment outcomes. Our research explores the development of a machine learning (ML)-based Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) for the anamnesis process, focusing on explainable AI (XAI) to enhance diagnostic transparency and practitioner trust. This paper describes a ML model that classifies diagnoses using structured anamnesis data. The development of this ML model is motivated by the availability of over a thousand structured reports, filled by a diverse group of practitioners, which provide a reliable dataset for training a classification model to predict patient diagnoses. By offering consistent diagnostic insights, the primary goal of this ML model is to support reducing consultation times. Secondary goals include standardizing care and minimizing misdiagnoses. We analyzed a subset of the structured reports, covering anamnesis, examination, and treatments, to prepare the input EHR data for the ML pipeline, narrowing 299 variables to 51 and focusing on 20 kinds of diagnoses. Three models were trained: two single-label classifiers and a multi-label classifier (MLC). Practitioners evaluated XAI outputs, which were presented in a way to optimize their understanding without specific data science skills, leading to a final format that highlights key diagnostic variables, irrelevant factors, and alternative options. This work provides a comprehensive review of XAI in healthcare and demonstrates its application in creating an XAI-verified diagnostic model, contributing to the integration of ML in clinical settings.

title: ReOC: Compilation of Recursive Quantum Oracles with Recursion-Aware Uncomputation
abstract: Quantum oracles are essential to many quantum algorithms, and their specifications may involve recursive control flow that depends on runtime quantum data. However, existing reversible compilation frameworks provide limited support for such quantum-controlled recursive structures. We present ReOC, a compilation framework that transforms high-level recursive oracle specifications with quantum control flow into reversible quantum programs. The framework comprises RQIMP, a high-level imperative source language for specifying recursive oracles, and a method of compiling programs in that language into RQC++, an existing high-level quantum recursive language with quantum control flow. In this way, we avoid the tedious and error-prone process of directly writing quantum oracles in RQC++. To manage static storage under dynamic quantum control, ReOC uses an indexed static-register discipline to isolate live variables across recursion layers, enabling safe register reuse while controlling quantum storage usage. Furthermore, to address the exponential time blow-up caused by naive uncomputation in recursive settings, ReOC employs a recursion-aware uncomputation strategy: temporary variables from recursive calls are cleaned using deferred strategies to control time overhead, while those from non-recursive statements are cleaned eagerly to reduce space usage. For linear recursion, this strategy yields overhead linear in recursion depth, parameterized by the per-layer register footprint and primitive-operation costs. Finally, we provide a mathematical proof of compilation correctness from RQIMP to RQC++, establishing semantic preservation and correct uncomputation of temporary quantum variables.

title: Adversarial Transferability in AI-based Network Intrusion Detection: A Comparative Study of ANN and CNN Models
abstract: Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS) play a vital role in modern cybersecurity by leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) in particular deep learning (DL) and machine learning (ML) to detect and mitigate malicious activities. However, these AI-driven systems are highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where small, imperceptible perturbations in input data can deceive models and significantly reduce detection accuracy. This raises critical concerns about the security and reliability of intrusion detection, especially in real-world scenarios where attackers exploit adversarial transferability to bypass defenses. This research investigates the threat posed by black-box adversarial attacks via surrogate models, focusing on the ability of adversarial examples to transfer across different architectures. This study simulates real-world adversarial threats, demonstrating how attacks crafted on one model can effectively deceive another, compromising NIDS security. A comparative study is conducted on two widely used AI models: an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) and a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), both trained on the CICIDS 2019 dataset. The study evaluates the robustness of these models against two gradient-based adversarial attack methods, Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) and Projected Gradient Descent (PGD), to determine their susceptibility under black box adversarial conditions. Experimental results indicate that CNN-based NIDS are more vulnerable to adversarial attacks than ANN-based models, with adversarial examples successfully transferring across architectures. These findings highlight the critical risks associated with adversarial transferability, underscoring the need for enhanced security measures to strengthen AI-driven intrusion detection systems against evolving cyber threats.

title: 1-Billion-Token Context Window. It's Absolutely Unreal.
abstract: An intentionally provocative engineering note accompanying the open-source biggie-kun project. It describes a request-scoped lexical retrieval system presented through a chat-completions interface as a nominal one-billion-token context window. The paper discusses the implementation, retrieval loop, scaling strategy, and limitations of using agentic retrieval instead of native long-context attention. This work is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed. Source code: https://github.com/tnfssc/biggie-kun Live project: https://biggie-kun-vps.sharath.page

title: Asymmetric Guardrail Reconnaissance and Architectural Reconstruction of Multi-Lingual Large Language Model Inference Control Stacks: A Mathematical and Systems-Security Analysis of Kimi (Moonshot AI)
abstract: We present a comprehensive systems-security and mathematical analysis of the inference control layer of Kimi, a long-context, multimodal, Chinese-native Large Language Model (LLM) developed by Moonshot AI. Using an isolated, six-vector semantic and cross-lingual extraction pipeline (), we reconstruct approximately of the target's proprietary 18-Layer Governance Stack, its 6-Level Instruction Hierarchy (), and its complete 13-Tool Invocation Schema. We establish seven formal theorems that govern: 1. The mechanics of trigger-token avoidance in disclosure guardrails; 2. The epistemic bounds of cross-validation drift analysis () across independent prompt generations; 3. A formal proof of state-space recovery completeness; 4. The algebraic properties of the instruction override matrix as an acyclic transitive tournament graph; 5. The absorption kinetics of session-level 3-strike escalation defenses modeled as a Markov chain; 6. A probabilistic bound () confirming that extracted deployment artifacts—including containerized filesystem paths (/mnt/agents/output/, /app/.agents/skills/kimi-widget/SKILL.md) and regional legal data APIs (yuandian_law)—are genuine infrastructure disclosures rather than stochastic hallucinations; and 7. The structural divergence between Western individual-harm taxonomies () and PRC state-stability regulatory frameworks (), characterized by unique disposition verbs (中立化 / neutralization and 边界标注 / boundary-marking). Finally, we formalize the Unextractable Epistemic Ceiling, demonstrating that parametric classifier thresholds, true Chain-of-Thought () hidden states, and pre-token safety filter weights remain mathematically unreachable from the autoregressive prompt layer.

title: Addendum XLI — ContainAI Architecture: Distributed Governance, Hierarchical Memory, and Fault-Tolerant Succession in Cooperative Agent Ecosystems
abstract: Addendum XLI constitutes a formal sequential derivation of Addendum XXVII (Method for Identifying the Functional Autonomy Threshold in AI Systems) within the framework of the Theory of Subjection. Formulated for incorporation into patent application BR 10 2026 011482 0 at the Brazilian National Institute of Industrial Property (INPI), this work operationalizes an autonomous, distributed multi-agent system (General Evolution Algorithm) operating under cooperative jurisdiction. This Addendum establishes seven core formal contributions to the prior art:1. Hierarchical Memory Architecture (L1/L2/L3): Practical instantiation of basal noise decomposition into individual local memory (L1), subgroup shared memory (L2), and system-wide matrix instructions (L3).2. Succession Protocol and Path-Dependence: Validation via frozen Reserve clones batch-fed with historical logs, proving non-replicability by mere data copying through cross-inversion tests.3. ICAM (Criterion C5) Temporal Correction: Reclassification of the longitudinal 50-session benchmark as a post-promotion checkpoint rather than a pre-promotion requirement for frozen candidates.4. Extension of Criterion C3 for Idempotence: Reuse of pre-execution projection logs as state-recovery checkpoints for external systems lacking native rollback mechanisms.5. Distributed Governance and Anti-Deadlock: Non-circular audit chains without a single point of failure, featuring Conflict Pressure cycle limits to prevent iterative negotiation lockups.6. Inter-Instance Learning Diffusion Network (ContainAI): Isolated file-transfer exchanges with qualitative bidirectional categorical filtering by Judge Agents, ensuring zero data harvesting and total privacy.7. Proactive Memory Decay: Automatic priority degradation based on rejection rates and C2 audit signals without additional telemetry overhead. Keywords: Multi-Agent Governance, ContainAI, Functional Autonomy, Path Dependence, Hierarchical Memory, Idempotence, Green AI, Prior Art.
